chunks: Printing features smaller than the wavelength. The question: Some feature sizes may be in the nm range, but the wavelengths of light used may not be in that same range.
How are these small feature sizes created?
The smallest feature you can print is not set by the wavelength of light alone. The lens and the process matter too.
With clever optics, computer-corrected stencils (masks), and extra steps that add and remove thin films, factories print lines spaced about 20 nm apart using 193 nm light.
A newer light, extreme ultraviolet (EUV) at 13. 5 nm, prints the finest layers in one exposure.
Imagine you want thin lines but own only a fat marker. Draw fat stripes first. Paint a thin coat down both edges of every stripe, then wipe the stripes away.
Each stripe leaves two thin lines, so the lines are twice as dense as the marker could draw. This is pitch division. The line width comes from the coat, not the marker.
Interference of the two beams makes bright and dark fringes every 71. 5 nm, less than half of the 193 nm free-space wavelength.
Resist acts as a threshold (dashed line): where intensity exceeds it, the resist is exposed; below it, not.
The fringes can be arbitrarily precise in position but the pitch cannot go below λ/(2NA); with a single exposure, beyond that the 1st order is outside the lens aperture and no fringes form.
Drag NA down to 0. 8, as in a dry lens, and the period grows to about 120 nm; drag the wavelength down toward 150 nm and the fringes tighten in proportion.
Wavelength: the distance between peaks of a light wave. Numerical aperture (NA): how wide an angle of light the lens collects.
Pitch: the center-to-center distance between repeating lines. Half-pitch is half of that. Immersion: water between the lens and wafer, which raises the NA above 1.
Spacer: a thin film left standing on the side wall of a printed line.
For one exposure, the smallest half-pitch is about 0. 25 times wavelength ÷ NA. With 193 nm light and immersion at NA 1. 35, that is 0. 25 times 193 ÷ 1.
35 about 36 nm, a pitch of about 72 nm. To go finer, print lines at an easy 80 nm pitch. Coat them evenly, one atomic layer at a time.
Etch the coat back so only the spacers on the side walls remain, and remove the original lines. Now the pitch is 40 nm. Repeat once more and it is 20 nm. That is the whole idea.
"Resolution isn't set by wavelength alone: it's k 1 over NA .

With 193 nm light you push NA above 1 using water immersion, lower k1 with OPC, phase-shift masks and off-axis illumination, and then go beyond the single-exposure limit with multiple patterning, where spacers deposited by ALD and etched back divide the pitch by two or four.
EUV at 13. 5 nm does it in one shot for the finest layers. And node names aren't real feature sizes."
